extracted.intended_audience: readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal (mathematicians, advanced students interested in analytic geometry, statics, and numerical methods)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and formulae for (a) computing logarithms/antilogarithms and (b) deriving coordinates of centres of gravity for lines, polygons, surfaces, pyramids and polyhedra, together with algebraic criteria for classifying and constructing second-degree (quadratic) surfaces tangent to given planes or inscribed in tetrahedra/parallelepipeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-logarithm extraction using tabular differences
rubrics_metrics.description: After rejecting the index, refer to the first table of the 'Anti-Logarithmic' set and note the logarithm next less than the given one. Then put down the difference; then note the log. in ii. next less than this difference and subtract it, putting down the second difference, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By this means we determine a series of factors which may be multiplied with the greatest ease, and thus the number is determined. The worked example shows successive subtraction of the nearest lesser table entries to produce factors that are multiplied to recover the anti-logarithm; avoid rewriting already settled figures to save labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the index to determine digit count when finding a number from its log
rubrics_metrics.description: The index indicates the order of magnitude (number of digits) of the number: e.g. 'The index being 9 the number consists of ten digits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the index when forming the anti-log process described above (i.e., treat the mantissa only) and then restore the index to place the decimal point appropriately after computing the product of factors from the anti-log tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical method for forming logarithms (numerical algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the logarithm of a number to a required number of places by a sequence of multiplications and table lookups producing successive partial results and remainders (illustrated by the worked example for log 48.76 to six places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successive multiplications of remainders and reference to appropriate log tables give digits of the mantissa step by step; the worked table-headed columns (I., II., III., ...) show how to iterate to the desired precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a composite body (general weighted-average formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If parts have weights w, w', w'' and centres with coordinates x y z, x' y' z', x'' y'' z'', then the coordinates of the whole body are x̄ = (w x + w' x' + w'' x'' + ...)/(w + w' + w'' + ...), and similarly for ȳ and z̄.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the theory of parallel forces. When all component weights are equal the formula reduces to the simple arithmetic mean of the component coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a straight line coincides with the centre (midpoint) of two equal weights placed at its extremities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain coordinates by setting n = 2 in the general weighted-average formula: coordinates are the averages of the endpoints' coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of the perimeter of a polygon
rubrics_metrics.description: If the polygon has angular points with coordinates and the centres of its sides have coordinates obtained as averages of adjacent vertices, then the centre of gravity of the perimeter is the weighted average of the side-centres with weights proportional to side lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equations (2) (the perimeter formulae) and, when the polygon lies in a plane, take that plane as the xy-plane and determine the centre from the first two coordinate equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a triangular plate (uniform thickness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a triangular plate coincides with the centre of gravity of three equal weights placed at its angular points; i.e., the centroid is the average of the three vertices' coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain from the general formula by taking n = 3; coordinates = (x + x' + x'')/3, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a planar figure (by decomposition into triangles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the polygonal area into triangles by joining a chosen point to the remote angular points; the centre of gravity of the figure is the weighted average of the centroids of those triangles with weights proportional to their areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write coordinates of each triangle-centroid (averages of its vertices), compute triangle areas (weights), then use the weighted-average formula. If all sides lie in one plane, use the first two coordinates only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a triangular pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a triangular pyramid coincides with the centre of gravity of four equal weights placed at its angular points; i.e., the centroid is the average of the four vertices' coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take n = 4 in the general formula to obtain x̄ = (x1 + x2 + x3 + x4)/4, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a polyhedron (decomposition into tetrahedra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the polyhedron into triangular pyramids (tetrahedra) whose weights are proportional to their volumes and compute the coordinates of the whole as the weighted average of each pyramid's centroid: x̄ = [Σ w_i (x_i + x'_i + x''_i + x'''_i)] / [4 Σ w_i], etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express pyramid volumes in terms of vertex coordinates so that equations (6) determine the polyhedron's centroid as functions of its vertices' coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between centroid of vertices and centroid of surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of a system of equal weights placed at the angular points of a polygon is, in general, different from the centre of gravity of its surface; they coincide only for a triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume vertex-average equals area-centroid except in the triangular case; the paper explicitly corrects a mistaken impression in earlier literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic method for discriminating the nature of a quadratic surface (use of factorization U = V W)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the general second-degree surface U and set U = V W with V and W quadratic forms whose coefficients ai and a'i are roots of a quadratic. Equations (1) and (4) (resulting relations) determine ai, a' and thus the nature of the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the properties of the resulting quadratic in a coordinate (e.g. in z), multiplicity and reality of roots classify the surface: equal roots correspond to a cone (rectilinear intersection planes coincide), a single essential root to hyperbolic paraboloid, real unequal roots to hyperboloid of one sheet (or two sheets when signs differ), etc. Examples illustrate the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of resolvability into sum or difference of two squares
rubrics_metrics.description: A second-degree form in two variables is resolvable into the sum or difference of two squares when certain algebraic relations among coefficients hold (derivable from comparing to a canonical squared-sum expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice express coefficients as squares A, B (and possibly C) and impose the derived equalities (e.g. 4BX1−F)(1+m^2) = B'(…); this resolvability is used to decide whether a tangent section is a point, two straight lines or a complete square (cone/cylinder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation to surfaces of second order touching three given planes
rubrics_metrics.description: Surfaces tangent to three given planes may be written in the form AV + BV + CW + cross-terms (see equations (6) and (6')), where setting one coordinate to zero yields an expression resolvable into the sum or difference of two squares; the signs and magnitudes of A,B,C and angular parameters dictate the surface type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coefficients have appropriate signs and are real, (6) denotes hyperboloids of one sheet or hyperbolic paraboloids; (6') denotes the other surfaces. Tangency conditions require that substitution of each coordinate-plane produce the stated resolvability; cones/cylinders arise as limiting cases when certain coefficients become very large or a square vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude parameter values that cause degeneracy when constructing tangent surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain algebraic parameter choices (e.g. a specific value of n) make the constructed quadratic equivalent to the sum or difference of two squares and thus degenerate to a straight line or two planes, which must be rejected when seeking genuine surfaces of the second order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the derivation of the family of surfaces touching given planes some roots/choices produce degenerate geometries and must be identified and excluded to obtain non-degenerate quadratic surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation to surfaces of second order inscribed in a tetrahedron (touching four planes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general equation to surfaces touching the four faces of a tetrahedron can be represented in symmetric form (equations (9) and (10)/(10')) with constraints among angle/parameter quantities (e.g. condition a/β = 1 or equivalent trigonometric relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must determine auxiliary parameters (/ , m, n, etc.) by putting coordinates to zero in turn and enforcing resolvability into sums/differences of squares; the resulting parameter relations (including trigonometric forms) must hold for a valid inscribed surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and classification of surfaces tangent to faces of a parallelepiped
rubrics_metrics.description: Let faces be written ±a, ±b, ±c about the centre (intersection of diagonals); substitute translated coordinates into the general three-plane-tangent form and eliminate coefficients to obtain the existence condition (equation (14)/(14')).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resulting condition gives the family of second-degree surfaces touching the given parallelepiped faces and shows their centres coincide with the intersection of the diagonals: the centre of all such inscribed quadratic surfaces is fixed at that point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of centres of surfaces of second order inscribed in a parallelepiped
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given parallelepiped, the centres of all second-order surfaces inscribed (touching the faces) coincide at the intersection point of the diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric reasoning: surfaces touching opposite parallel faces have centres on planes equidistant from those faces; the three such planes intersect at the diagonal intersection, hence the locus degenerates to that single point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone as limiting homogeneous quadratic (vertex at coordinate origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: When coefficients A, B, C are considered infinitely large relative to the linear/constant terms, the general touching-surface equation becomes homogeneous and represents a cone whose vertex is at the origin determined by u=0, v=0, w=0; the coordinate planes remain tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of coefficients' magnitudes yields degenerate families (cones/cylinders); check tangency by substituting coordinate planes and verifying the intersection becomes a straight line (complete square) or two coincident lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for summing trigonometric series via inverse-trigonometric differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Express terms of certain cosecant/cotangent-form series as differences of inverse-trigonometric functions (e.g. cos^{-1} differences) so the partial sums telescope and yield closed-form expressions which can be chosen to be squares for prescribed truncations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution demonstrates expressing general nth-term forms so that S_n = i cos^{-1}(...) etc., and constructs series whose infinite sum, finite-n sum, and tail-sum are all perfect squares by appropriate choice of parameters and identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application methods for statics problems (example: spiral for uniform ring motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive the required geometric form (spiral) of a wire so that a ring sliding on a fixed rod experiences uniform vertical motion by applying vis viva, expressing energy relations, setting dr/dt substitutions, and solving the resulting differential equation to obtain the spiral equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use energy (vis viva) relations to relate radial velocity and position, make substitutions to integrate (e.g. set r-dependent terms to functions like u^2), and solve for r(t) or for the polar equation of the spiral as demonstrated in the worked solution.
